screens.title: Writing and Compiling Smart Contracts with Truffle
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn to write a simple Solidity smart contract inside a Truffle project, run Truffle's compilation, and read the build artifacts that result. You'll see how a small contract demonstrates core concepts: a state variable, a constructor, a mutating function that requires a transaction, and a view function that reads state without gas. We'll also cover how the pragma directive must match or be compatible with the configured compiler version, why that matters for successful compilation, and what to look for inside the JSON file Truffle creates. By the end you will be able to create SimpleStorage. sol, run truffle compile, and locate the abi and bytecode that front-ends and deployments rely on. A concrete example will walk through the exact code for a storage contract, then show the command output and the structure of the build artifact. As you work, pay attention to two common traps: compiler version mismatch and simple syntax errors. Which of these errors is most likely to block your build when you first try compiling?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This chapter has four clear objectives that map to doing, not just knowing. First, you will recall the Solidity syntax and contract structure needed to write a simple contract that Truffle can compile. That means you can identify state variables, the constructor, and public functions. Second, you will create a file named SimpleStorage. sol and place it in the Truffle project's contracts directory so Truffle recognizes it. Third, you will run the truffle compile command and interpret successful compile output. Finally, you will open the generated build artifact JSON and find the abi and bytecode so you can wire that contract into a front-end or a deployment script. Each objective includes a small reason why it matters: compilation is the gatekeeper to deployment, and the ABI is the interface for integrations. Practice reading artifacts now so you are confident before moving to deployment.

screens.title: Truffle project layout and the contracts directory
screens.narratorSegment: A Truffle project has a predictable layout and Truffle expects your Solidity source files to live in the contracts directory. This convention matters because truffle compile scans that folder and automatically compiles files it finds. A well-organized contracts directory reduces errors and makes it clear which contracts belong to the project. As a concrete example, creating a file named SimpleStorage. sol inside contracts/ ensures Truffle compiles it and outputs build/contracts/SimpleStorage. json. A common misconception is that any file in the project root will be compiled; in practice, Truffle compiles files in contracts/ or those referenced by imports originating there. If you split contracts into subfolders, keep import paths consistent and relative so the compiler can resolve dependencies. A quick verification after compilation is to look for the JSON artifact with the same base name in build/contracts. That artifact is your proof of compilation success and the source for ABI and bytecode. How will you structure your contracts folder to keep imports simple? Truffle project layout and the contracts directory means place your solidity source files in contracts/ and use relative import paths so truffle compiles them into build/contracts/. In practical terms, how truffle discovers solidity source files and organizes compiled artifacts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Project file tree
Truffle looks for source files inside contracts/ and writes artifacts into build/contracts/.

Why this matters
Truffle's conventions make compilation predictable and make it easy to find the artifact you need for deployment and front-end calls.
Common mistake
Saving a .sol file outside contracts/ will not be compiled unless imported from within contracts/.
Concrete example
// File: contracts/SimpleStorage.sol // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT pragma solidity ^0.8.19; contract SimpleStorage { uint256 public storedData; constructor() { storedData = 0; } function set(uint256 x) public { storedData = x; } function get() public view returns (uint256) { return storedData; } }
Key Takeaway

Keep source files in contracts/ and name them clearly so Truffle compiles and produces a matching artifact in build/contracts/.

screens.title: SimpleStorage.sol explained line by line
screens.narratorSegment: We'll walk through the SimpleStorage contract to connect each line to its role. The pragma directive specifies the compiler version range the contract expects. The contract declares a public state variable named storedData of type unsigned 256-bit integer; making it public implicitly creates a getter function for external reads. The constructor initializes storedData to zero and runs once during deployment. The set function accepts an unsigned integer and assigns it to storedData. Because set changes state it must be executed as a transaction and will consume gas. The get function is marked view and returns storedData; it does not modify state and costs no gas when called externally. A concrete example: calling set with 42 will change storedData to 42; subsequently calling get returns 42. A common misconception is that public variables are free to write—public only affects visibility; writing still requires a transaction. Consider how visibility, state, and gas costs together determine how you design contract interactions. SimpleStorage.sol explained line by line means pragma enforces compiler compatibility; state variables persist on-chain; view functions read state without gas; mutators require transactions and gas.. In practical terms, read the contract, identify state, constructor, and functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Annotated code
1 // SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
2 pragma solidity ^0.8.19; // compiler version
3
4 contract SimpleStorage {
5   uint256 public storedData; // state variable + getter
6
7   constructor() { storedData = 0; } // runs once on deploy
8
9   function set(uint256 x) public { storedData = x; } // mutates state, requires gas
10
11   function get() public view returns (uint256) { return storedData; } // reads state, no gas when called externally
12 }
Concrete scenario
If you call set(42) in a transaction, storedData becomes 42; calling get afterwards returns 42 without gas when executed as a call.
Common misconception
Marking a variable public does not make writes free. Public exposes a getter; write operations still require transactions and gas.
Practical checks
  • Confirm the pragma version is compatible with Truffle's solc setting.
  • Ensure functions that change state will be invoked via transactions in tests or migrations.
  • Use view functions for reads to avoid unnecessary gas consumption.
Key Takeaway

Reading code line by line ties each Solidity construct to its runtime behavior: storage, gas, and visibility.

screens.title: Pragma and compiler version compatibility
screens.narratorSegment: The pragma solidity line declares the compiler versions a contract expects. In the SimpleStorage example we use pragma solidity ^0.8.19 which means the code is compatible with 0.8.19 and later patch/minor releases up to 0.9.0. This is important because language changes between major Solidity versions can break code or introduce different compiler behaviors. A frequent compilation error arises when the pragma in source does not match the solc version Truffle is configured to use. When that happens Truffle will abort compilation and display a message indicating the mismatch and the pragma line. You have two safe choices to resolve a mismatch: update the pragma in your contract to match the configured compiler, or change Truffle's solc version in truffle-config. js to a version compatible with the pragma. A misconception is to arbitrarily pin to the newest compiler; instead, choose a version compatible with your code and project dependencies, and test for any behavior changes. Which option you pick depends on whether your code relies on language features introduced in a specific major version. Pragma and compiler version compatibility means resolve pragma mismatches by aligning your contract's pragma with truffle's solc setting or vice versa to ensure successful compilation.. In practical terms, why the pragma directive must match truffle's configured solc. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Pragma & Compiler
What pragma means
Pragma specifies which compiler versions the source is compatible with and prevents accidental compilation with incompatible solc versions.
Example pragma
pragma solidity ^0.8.19;
The caret means compatible with 0.8.19 and higher 0.8.x patch releases, but not 0.9.0.
Resolution options
  • Update the pragma in the contract to match your Truffle solc version.
  • Or change truffle-config.js to use a solc version compatible with the pragma.
Common compilation error
SyntaxError: Source file requires different compiler version (current compiler is 0.8.19). Pragma statement: pragma solidity ^0.7.0;
Misconception
Changing the pragma without validating behavior can introduce subtle bugs; prefer aligning toolchain versions or testing changes carefully.
Key Takeaway

Treat pragma as a contract promise to the compiler; resolve mismatches by aligning configuration or code and then recompile.

screens.title: Compiling with Truffle
screens.narratorSegment: Compiling a contract with Truffle is an explicit two-step developer action: run truffle compile from your project root and then inspect the output. The compile command invokes solc, compiles each. sol file found in contracts/, and writes JSON artifacts to build/contracts/. A practical terminal sequence is to change to your project folder and run truffle compile. On success you will see lines indicating which contracts were compiled and where the artifacts were written. If compilation fails, Truffle prints error details including file and line numbers to help debug syntax or pragma issues. For an example, after saving SimpleStorage. sol in contracts/, running truffle compile should produce build/contracts/SimpleStorage. json. The concrete check is opening that JSON in your editor and confirming the presence of abi and bytecode fields. A useful habit is running compile often as you code, so errors are surfaced close to the change that introduced them. What will you open first when compilation completes: the terminal or the artifact? Compiling with Truffle means run truffle compile regularly. successful compilation produces build artifacts you will use for deployment and integration.. In practical terms, run the compile command and read the terminal output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Build artifacts: ABI and bytecode
screens.narratorSegment: After a successful compilation Truffle writes a JSON artifact for each contract. Two pieces are essential: the ABI and the bytecode. The ABI is a JSON array describing a contract's functions, their parameters, return types, and events. It tells external applications how to encode function calls and decode return data; without it a front-end cannot correctly call or interpret contract methods. Bytecode is the low-level machine code the EVM executes. When you deploy a contract the bytecode is sent to the network and stored on-chain as the contract's runtime code. The artifact may also include other helpful metadata such as the compiler version, the deployed bytecode, and a source map for debugging. A common misconception is to treat ABI and bytecode as interchangeable; they are distinct: the ABI is the interface description, while bytecode is the executable representation. The practical test is to open SimpleStorage. json and confirm abi is an array and bytecode is a string representing compiled code. Build artifacts: ABI and bytecode means abi describes the contract interface for callers; bytecode is the compiled code that the evm executes when deployed.. In practical terms, understand the contents of the json file truffle generates. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Build Artifacts
ABI (Application Binary Interface)
A JSON array describing functions, events, and parameter types. Front-ends use it to encode calls and decode results.
"abi": [ { "inputs": [], "name": "get", "outputs": [ { "internalType": "uint256", "name": "", "type": "uint256" } ], "stateMutability": "view", "type": "function" }, ... ]
Why ABI matters
Without the ABI a web or script cannot format calls to contract functions correctly.
Bytecode
Bytecode is the compiled machine code that the EVM executes. It appears as a long hex string in the artifact.
"bytecode": "0x6080604052..."
Misconception
The ABI is not executable code; it only describes the interface. The bytecode is what gets deployed.
Key Takeaway

Open the artifact and confirm an abi array and bytecode string exist. Use the ABI for integration and bytecode for deployment.

screens.title: View functions versus state-changing functions
screens.narratorSegment: Smart contracts include both read-only functions and functions that change state. In SimpleStorage the get function is marked view and returns storedData without modifying state. Calling a view function externally does not require a transaction and therefore does not consume gas. In contrast, the set function assigns a new value to storedData and therefore changes the contract's state; invoking it requires sending a transaction and paying gas. A concrete example: if you want to display the current stored value in a UI, call get as a free read. If you want to update the value to 100, call set in a transaction and expect to pay gas and wait for a mined block. A common misconception is that calling a view in a transaction will be entirely free; while the function itself does not change state, wrapping it in a transaction still consumes gas because the transaction submission and mining have costs. Always design the UI to use view calls for reads and transactions only for intentional writes. View functions versus state-changing functions means use view functions for reads to avoid gas where possible. mutators require transactions and will consume gas when executed.. In practical terms, understand gas costs and when to use each. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › View vs Mutator
View (get)
Marked view. Reads state, no gas for external calls. Use for UI displays.
function get() public view returns (uint256) { return storedData; }
Example: calling get after set(7) returns 7 immediately without gas when executed as a call.
Mutator (set)
Changes blockchain state and requires a transaction which consumes gas and waits for confirmation.
function set(uint256 x) public { storedData = x; }
Example: invoking set(100) sends a transaction; after mining get will return 100. Expect gas cost and block confirmation time.
Pitfall
Wrapping a view call in a transaction is unnecessary and may lead developers to pay gas for an operation that could have been done as a free call.
Key Takeaway

Design interactions to use view calls for reads and transactions for writes to keep costs clear to users.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn to write a simple Solidity smart contract inside a Truffle project, run Truffle's compilation, and read the build artifacts that result. You'll see how a small contract demonstrates core concepts: a state variable, a constructor, a mutating function that requires a transaction, and a view function that reads state without gas. We'll also cover how the pragma directive must match or be compatible with the configured compiler version, why that matters for successful compilation, and what to look for inside the JSON file Truffle creates. By the end you will be able to create SimpleStorage. sol, run truffle compile, and locate the abi and bytecode that front-ends and deployments rely on. A concrete example will walk through the exact code for a storage contract, then show the command output and the structure of the build artifact. As you work, pay attention to two common traps: compiler version mismatch and simple syntax errors. Which of these errors is most likely to block your build when you first try compiling?

This chapter has four clear objectives that map to doing, not just knowing. First, you will recall the Solidity syntax and contract structure needed to write a simple contract that Truffle can compile. That means you can identify state variables, the constructor, and public functions. Second, you will create a file named SimpleStorage. sol and place it in the Truffle project's contracts directory so Truffle recognizes it. Third, you will run the truffle compile command and interpret successful compile output. Finally, you will open the generated build artifact JSON and find the abi and bytecode so you can wire that contract into a front-end or a deployment script. Each objective includes a small reason why it matters: compilation is the gatekeeper to deployment, and the ABI is the interface for integrations. Practice reading artifacts now so you are confident before moving to deployment.

Let's expand the objectives into concrete practice. For recalling Solidity structure, open the example SimpleStorage code and say aloud the role of each line: state variable, constructor, setter, and getter. A helpful mnemonic is S. C. A. R: State, Constructor, Actions, Read functions. For creating the file, remember to save it in contracts/ using a descriptive name so Truffle compiles it automatically. When running truffle compile, note both success lines and warnings: the command writes JSON artifacts into build/contracts/. To inspect artifacts, open the JSON and look for the abi array and the bytecode string; they are the pieces you will reference in deployment scripts and front-end web3 calls. Each objective also includes a small verification step: after compiling, find SimpleStorage. json and confirm that abi is present and non-empty. This practice cements both the mental model and the practical check you will use repeatedly.

A Truffle project has a predictable layout and Truffle expects your Solidity source files to live in the contracts directory. This convention matters because truffle compile scans that folder and automatically compiles files it finds. A well-organized contracts directory reduces errors and makes it clear which contracts belong to the project. As a concrete example, creating a file named SimpleStorage. sol inside contracts/ ensures Truffle compiles it and outputs build/contracts/SimpleStorage. json. A common misconception is that any file in the project root will be compiled; in practice, Truffle compiles files in contracts/ or those referenced by imports originating there. If you split contracts into subfolders, keep import paths consistent and relative so the compiler can resolve dependencies. A quick verification after compilation is to look for the JSON artifact with the same base name in build/contracts. That artifact is your proof of compilation success and the source for ABI and bytecode. How will you structure your contracts folder to keep imports simple? Truffle project layout and the contracts directory means place your solidity source files in contracts/ and use relative import paths so truffle compiles them into build/contracts/. In practical terms, how truffle discovers solidity source files and organizes compiled artifacts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

We'll walk through the SimpleStorage contract to connect each line to its role. The pragma directive specifies the compiler version range the contract expects. The contract declares a public state variable named storedData of type unsigned 256-bit integer; making it public implicitly creates a getter function for external reads. The constructor initializes storedData to zero and runs once during deployment. The set function accepts an unsigned integer and assigns it to storedData. Because set changes state it must be executed as a transaction and will consume gas. The get function is marked view and returns storedData; it does not modify state and costs no gas when called externally. A concrete example: calling set with 42 will change storedData to 42; subsequently calling get returns 42. A common misconception is that public variables are free to write—public only affects visibility; writing still requires a transaction. Consider how visibility, state, and gas costs together determine how you design contract interactions. SimpleStorage.sol explained line by line means pragma enforces compiler compatibility; state variables persist on-chain; view functions read state without gas; mutators require transactions and gas.. In practical terms, read the contract, identify state, constructor, and functions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The pragma solidity line declares the compiler versions a contract expects. In the SimpleStorage example we use pragma solidity ^0.8.19 which means the code is compatible with 0.8.19 and later patch/minor releases up to 0.9.0. This is important because language changes between major Solidity versions can break code or introduce different compiler behaviors. A frequent compilation error arises when the pragma in source does not match the solc version Truffle is configured to use. When that happens Truffle will abort compilation and display a message indicating the mismatch and the pragma line. You have two safe choices to resolve a mismatch: update the pragma in your contract to match the configured compiler, or change Truffle's solc version in truffle-config. js to a version compatible with the pragma. After a successful compilation Truffle writes a JSON artifact for each contract. Two pieces are essential: the ABI and the bytecode. The ABI is a JSON array describing a contract's functions, their parameters, return types, and events. It tells external applications how to encode function calls and decode return data; without it a front-end cannot correctly call or interpret contract methods. Bytecode is the low-level machine code the EVM executes. When you deploy a contract the bytecode is sent to the network and stored on-chain as the contract's runtime code. Smart contracts include both read-only functions and functions that change state. In SimpleStorage the get function is marked view and returns storedData without modifying state.
